rationale: Job and Noah are both introduced as righteous and blameless men before the accounts of calamity affecting their surroundings. The parallel concerns the narrators' character judgments, not an identification of the two men.
Ezekiel names Job alongside Noah and Daniel as an example of righteousness, corresponding to the prologue's description of Job as righteous, blameless and God-fearing.

The appendix again locates Job in Ausitis and adds its borders and the former name Jobab. This links the book's opening identification with its own closing identification without independently verifying the appendix's historical claims.

The seven sons and three daughters in the opening household correspond numerically to the seven sons and three daughters born to Job at the close. The later verse does not identify them as the children who died.
The closing inventory doubles each opening livestock total: sheep, camels, pairs of oxen and female donkeys. Both passages explicitly enumerate the same four categories of Job's wealth.
The recurring feasts involving Job's sons and daughters establish the family pattern repeated when the children gather to drink wine in their elder brother's house on the day of the losses.

Job offers sacrifices for his children because they may have entertained evil thoughts toward God; later God directs his friends to obtain an offering and prayer through Job after their false speech. Both passages present Job interceding for others.

Both scenes place heavenly beings before the Lord and include a spirit whose subsequent harmful activity occurs under an expressed commission or limit. The lying spirit in Micaiah's vision is not identified as Job's devil.

Job's devil appears in the assembly before the Lord, while Zechariah's slanderer stands beside Joshua to oppose him and receives the Lord's rebuke. Both scenes situate hostile spiritual opposition before divine authority.
The devil describes traveling around the earth in Job; Peter describes the devil walking about in search of someone to devour. The shared roaming image accompanies the adversary's threatening role.
The second heavenly scene repeats the Lord's question about the devil's origin and the devil's report of walking through the world, recalling this first exchange.

The Lord's assessment of Job repeats the opening narrator's description of his innocence, truthfulness, fear of God and avoidance of evil. The coming losses are therefore not introduced as proof that Job was secretly wicked.
The Lord calls attention to Job's outstanding righteousness here; Ezekiel subsequently names Job among three righteous men whose own righteousness would deliver them in the judgment described there.

The first accusation asks whether Job's worship is disinterested; the second argues that preserving his life explains his endurance and proposes bodily harm. Both accusations challenge the motive behind his fidelity.

The devil questions whether Job worships without reward, but after losing his possessions and children Job blesses the Lord and the narrator reports no sin. The ending of this trial answers the accusation through Job's response.
The devil describes divine protection around Job's household and abundant possessions; Job later remembers God's guarding care, attention to his house, children around him and former abundance.
The first proposal predicts that taking Job's possessions will make him curse God; the second repeats that prediction while shifting the proposed blow to his bones and flesh.
The first permission excludes touching Job himself, whereas the second hands Job over but requires preservation of his life. The two scenes state different limits on the devil's activity.

Job's trial proceeds after the devil's proposal and the Lord's limited permission. Jesus likewise speaks of Satan demanding to sift the disciples and of His prayer that Simon's faith not fail; the outcomes and limits are not identical.
The children drinking together in the elder brother's house repeats the family feasting pattern already described, identifying the ordinary gathering interrupted by the ensuing disaster.

The first messenger names oxen and female donkeys, two of the livestock categories enumerated in Job's opening inventory. His report begins to connect the particular losses with that earlier account of wealth.

Both reports describe attackers carrying off livestock, killing servants with swords and leaving one messenger to report. This edition calls the first attackers raiders and the later attackers horsemen, without identifying them as the same attacking group.

Job's messenger reports fire falling from heaven and consuming sheep and shepherds; the Elijah account describes fire from heaven consuming military companies. The similar description does not establish the same cause or moral status for the victims.
The horsemen's attack repeats the earlier report's combination of stolen livestock, servants killed with swords and a sole surviving messenger, while involving camels rather than the earlier animals.

The messenger recalls Job's sons and daughters eating together immediately before the collapse reported next; Job's wife later mourns those sons and daughters as the vanished memorial for whom she labored.

The house's collapse kills Job's children; his wife's later lament specifically recalls the loss of the sons and daughters she bore. Her speech gives the mother's perspective on this reported catastrophe.

The deaths of Job's children precede the closing report that seven sons and three daughters were born to him. The connection follows the household's loss and later renewal without asserting that the later children are the same individuals.
Job tears his garments on receiving the reports, and his friends later tear their robes and weep when they see his condition. Both passages portray mourning through torn clothing.

Both Job and Ezra tear their garments and remove hair from their heads in distress. Job cuts his hair after bereavement, while Ezra plucks hair after hearing of covenant-breaking, so the shared gestures have different occasions.

Both passages describe coming naked from the mother's womb and departing as one came. Ecclesiastes emphasizes that no earnings can be carried away, corresponding to Job's acknowledgment that what was given can be taken.

Job contrasts his naked arrival and departure with the Lord's giving and taking; First Timothy says that nothing was brought into the world and nothing can be carried out. Both detach possessions from the beginning and end of life.
After the first losses the narrator says Job did not sin or attribute foolishness to God; after bodily affliction the narrator again reports that he did not sin with his lips before God.
The narrator's judgment that Job remained without sin through these losses supplies an episode of the endurance James explicitly recalls when naming Job and the Lord's compassionate outcome.
The second scene repeats the angels' appearance before the Lord and the devil's presence among them, reopening the setting in which the first trial was authorized.
The Lord again asks where the devil has come from, and the devil again reports traveling through the world. The repeated exchange frames the second challenge as a continuation of the first.

The Lord again describes Job's exceptional innocence and fear of God, now adding that he still holds his innocence after the destruction of his possessions. The earlier assessment is expressly maintained after the first test.

The devil claims that a person will pay whatever he possesses to preserve his life; Jesus asks what profit the whole world offers if life is forfeited and what can be given in exchange for life. The valuation is comparable without endorsing the devil's accusation.
The prediction that Job will curse God repeats the first proposal, but the object of the requested blow changes from possessions to bones and flesh. This identifies the second trial's escalation.
The Lord now permits harm to Job but requires that his life be preserved. The earlier permission placed his possessions in the devil's hand while forbidding harm to Job himself.

relationship: Close bodily description with contextual difference
rationale: Both passages describe a grievous ulcer extending from the feet toward the head. Deuteronomy places it among covenant curses, whereas Job's prologue explicitly calls him innocent; the shared description does not prove Job's guilt.

Job's ulcer is inflicted by the devil, while Paul describes a thorn in the flesh and a messenger of Satan striking him. Both connect affliction with hostile spiritual agency, but Paul's unspecified thorn is not identified as Job's ulcer.
The narrator describes Job scraping discharge with a potsherd; Job later describes his decaying body and scraping off its discharge. The later complaint recalls the same distinctive bodily action.

Job, introduced as wealthy, now sits on a dung heap; Lamentations describes people formerly nursed upon scarlet wrapping themselves in dung heaps. The unusual setting marks a collapse from former prosperity in both scenes.

Job's wife questions how long he will persist, whereas the Lord has just commended him for still holding to innocence. Her challenge and the divine assessment take different views of his continuing endurance.

His wife's quotation attributes to Job an expectation of deliverance; Job later says that speaking before God will become deliverance and that he expects to be shown righteous. Both passages explicitly voice that expectation.
The wife's lament names the sons and daughters she bore as lost; the earlier messenger reports the house collapsing on Job's children and killing them.

The wife describes Job among worm-decay through the night; his later complaint joins nights of pain with a body fouled by worm-decay and discharge. The correspondence concerns these particular features of the suffering.

The wife describes her own wandering hired service and waiting for sunset to rest; Job later compares human life to hired work and a servant obtaining shade. The later comparison is an image, not a claim that Job shares her employment.

The wife urges a word to the Lord and death; Job answers that good received from the Lord must be accompanied by bearing bad things. His response opposes her counsel, while this edition's phrase 'some word' is left unchanged.
Job's acceptance of bad as well as good from the Lord recalls his acknowledgment of the Lord's giving and taking. Both responses are followed by the narrator's statement that Job did not sin.
The three named friends arrive to comfort Job; the ending names the same men when God rebukes their speech and directs them to seek an offering and prayer through Job.
The appendix repeats the three friends' names and titles: Eliphaz king of the Temanites, Bildad ruler of the Shuhites and Zophar king of the Minaeans. It directly recalls the group introduced here.
The friends initially come to comfort Job, but he later calls them all comforters of evils. The later rebuke contrasts the stated purpose of their visit with Job's experience of their speech.
The friends' torn robes and grief correspond to Job's earlier tearing of garments after the losses. The friends now participate in outward mourning for the suffering they see.

The friends sit beside the afflicted Job for seven days and nights before speaking; Ezekiel sits among the exiles for seven days before the next divine word. Both narratives mark an extended seven-day presence before subsequent speech, without equating the events.
The friends initially refrain from speaking because of Job's great affliction. After their speeches, Job wishes that they would be silent and says that silence would count as wisdom for them.
Job opens his lament by cursing his day; Jeremiah explicitly curses the day of his birth. Both passages introduce a sufferer's repudiation of the day on which his life began.
Both laments curse the day of birth and recall the announcement of a male child. Job wishes the day and announcement-night to perish, while Jeremiah also curses the bearer of the birth announcement.

Job wishes his birth-day deprived of brightness; Amos depicts daylight becoming dark as festivals turn to mourning. The darkness accompanies anguish in both passages, but Amos's announced judgment is not identified with Job's birth-day.

Job wishes darkness and death's shadow to claim his birth-day; later he describes the destination before him as a gloomy land with no brightness. The later lament develops the same association between darkness and death.

Removing his birth-day from the calendar expresses Job's repudiation of his beginning. Later he wishes he had died unseen and become as though he had never existed, making the underlying wish explicit.
Job wishes the birth-night stripped of gladness and joy; Jeremiah curses the messenger who announced a boy's birth with rejoicing. Both laments reverse the joy normally attached to that announcement.

Job imagines a night waiting for light but receiving none; Amos warns those desiring the Lord's day that it is darkness without brightness. Both overturn an expectation of light, in distinct lament and judgment settings.
Job blames the night for failing to close the womb and spare him pain. Jeremiah likewise wishes he had died in the womb and asks why he emerged to experience labors and pains.
Job asks why he did not die as he emerged from the womb; later he repeats the question and imagines being taken directly from womb to tomb.

Job questions why he was received and nursed; the psalmist remembers being drawn from the womb and finding hope from his mother's breasts. The common birth-and-nursing imagery serves lament in Job and a plea grounded in former care in the psalm.

Job names breasts and welcoming knees while questioning his survival; Isaiah combines nursing at a comforting breast with children comforted on knees. The same nurturing images have contrasting emotional force.

Job imagines that early death would have meant lying quietly, sleeping and resting. Later he describes the person who lies down in death and does not wake from sleep until heaven is no longer stitched together.

Job imagines resting with kings and counselors of the earth; Isaiah's taunt depicts former rulers and kings meeting the fallen Babylonian king in Hades. Royal standing does not keep either passage's rulers from the company of the dead.
Job places rulers with houses full of silver among the dead. The psalm likewise describes those boasting in wealth, leaving it to strangers and having tombs as their enduring houses.

Job wishes for the condition of a miscarriage or infants who never saw light. Ecclesiastes similarly compares a troubled long life with a stillborn child who never saw the sun and is said to have more rest.

Job's second clause imagines rest for bodies worn out by suffering. Isaiah announces rest from pain and harsh slavery before a taunt over the fallen oppressor; the comparison concerns relief from suffering, not Job's separate clause about the ungodly's anger.

Job places small and great together where the servant no longer fears a master. Later he contrasts a prosperous death with a bitter one, then says both people sleep together in the earth and decay covers them.
Job asks why light and life are given to the bitter and suffering; Jeremiah asks why he left the womb to see labors and pains. Both laments question the purpose of continuing life under distress.

Job describes sufferers longing for death without obtaining it; Jonah asks the Lord to take his life because he regards death as better than living. The shared longing arises in different narrative circumstances and is not a command to readers.

Job pictures rejoicing if death is obtained, while Ecclesiastes, after describing extortion, praises the dead above those still living. Both passages express a sufferer's or observer's preference for death over distressing life.

Job describes God shutting a man in; the speaker in Lamentations describes God building against him, blocking his exit and obstructing his paths. Both use confinement to describe their experience of affliction.

The devil earlier described God's fencing around Job as protection for household and possessions. Job now experiences God's enclosing action as confinement, reversing the earlier account's favorable meaning.
Job describes sighing before his food and weeping under fear; the psalmist says tears became his bread day and night. Both connect sustained grief with the experience of eating.

Job says that feared trouble met him; later he recalls waiting for good things but meeting days of evils instead. Both recollections describe the arrival of calamity in relation to his earlier expectations.
Job says he has neither peace, quiet nor rest. His later complaint describes empty months and nights of pain, continually waiting for day or evening without relief.
